newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris farm show aims to promote meat consumption.
newsitem.headline: Paris farm show aims to promote meat consumption.

text.p: An international farm show in Paris next week wants to woo consumers back to meat after the scare over mad cow disease shook public confidence throughout Europe.

Farmers, butchers and experts will seek to persuade 600,000 visitors expected for the February 23-March 2 annual SIA show that efforts to guarantee product quality make it safe to eat French meat again.

Beef producers were hardest hit by the mad cow crisis that erupted last March, but the whole meat industry is mobilising at the show to help revive flagging consumption, Aime Savy, a spokesman for national meat board OFIVAL, told Reuters.
"We want to reassure consumers about the quality of French meat although we know it's a long shot," he said.
The industry has mounted a 50 million franc advertising campaign.
OFIVAL said its research showed the slump in beef eating last year did not significantly benefit other meats as the biggest shift was towards fish.
France was the first nation to ban imports of British beef after Britain announced a possible link between Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) and a fatal disease in humans.
In April it introduced a "French beef" logo to allay consumer fears but meat sales continued to fall.
The focus now is on quality and strict control of origin, with the introduction since January of a "controlled quality criteria" logo, farming officials say.
"The keyword is transparency. Consumers must be able to track down the meat from the farm to their plate," said Marie-Christine Scotta-Loisel, a spokeswoman for the Meat Information Centre.
Exhibitors will teach consumers to identify quality labels, OFIVAL said.
France's 26 reported cases of mad cow disease are modest compared with 160,000 in Britain.
But although beef is making a small comeback in French restaurants and homes, sales are still lagging, figures show.
In January, beef sales were down eight to 10 percent over year-earlier levels. Sales fell by 10 percent in 1996 over 1995, but that was less than in many European Union countries.
OFIVAL expects consumption to rise by five percent in 1997, barring further bad news in the mad cow saga. But consumption would still be below 1995 levels.
France had 21 million cows in 1996, Europe's largest cow population. The country is the leading beef producer in Europe and the second-largest milk producer after Germany.
